stem: A business **project** is best described as

options.content: a one-off task with an objective, a budget and an end date
options.rationale: Correct: it is temporary and aimed at a specific result.

options.content: a business activity repeated every day without any set end date
options.rationale: Routine work that has no end date is not a project.

options.content: a list of all the workers employed in a firm during the year
options.rationale: That is a staff list, not a project.

options.content: a loan from a bank that is repaid in equal monthly parts
options.rationale: A loan is a source of finance, not a project.

explanation: A project is a temporary undertaking with a clear objective, resources and a time limit.

stem: Which is the **correct order** of the stages of the project cycle?

options.content: Identification, formulation, implementation, evaluation
options.rationale: Correct: the cycle begins with an idea and ends with a review.

options.content: Evaluation, identification, implementation, formulation
options.rationale: Evaluation comes at the end, not the start.

options.content: Implementation, identification, evaluation, formulation
options.rationale: Implementation cannot precede identification and formulation.

options.content: Formulation, evaluation, identification, implementation
options.rationale: A project must be identified before it can be formulated.

explanation: The order is identification, formulation (proposal and plan), implementation and evaluation.

stem: What is the main purpose of a **project proposal**?

options.content: To record the profit made after the whole project ends
options.rationale: That belongs to the evaluation report.

options.content: To list the workers who will be dismissed at the end
options.rationale: A proposal does not list dismissals.

options.content: To replace the need for any plan or any budget at all
options.rationale: A plan and budget are still needed.

options.content: To persuade others to approve or to fund the project
options.rationale: Correct: it presents the idea and its benefits for approval.

explanation: A proposal is written to gain approval and support for the project.

stem: A group has found that three families in the area want to buy school jerseys but cannot find a nearby supplier. This is an example of which stage of the project cycle?

options.content: Evaluation of the results
options.rationale: Evaluation takes place after the project is completed.

options.content: Identification of the need
options.rationale: Correct: spotting a need or opportunity starts the cycle.

options.content: Implementation of the plan
options.rationale: Implementation follows the plan and proposal.

options.content: Writing the project budget
options.rationale: The budget is part of formulation.

explanation: Finding a need that could become a project is identification.

stem: A student team has strong sewing skills but very little money. Which project idea fits their resources best?

options.content: Opening a large restaurant with a rented kitchen and staff
options.rationale: A restaurant needs far more money and a different skill set.

options.content: Buying a minibus to run a long-distance transport route
options.rationale: A minibus needs large capital.

options.content: Drilling a borehole to supply water to a whole village
options.rationale: Drilling needs expensive equipment and expertise.

options.content: Mending clothes for local people using borrowed machines
options.rationale: Correct: it uses their skills and needs little start-up money.

explanation: Choose a project that matches skills and available funds.
hints: Match the idea to both the skills and the money available.

stem: Why should a project plan include a **contingency**?

options.content: To increase the profit the group makes from the project
options.rationale: A contingency is a reserve, not extra profit.

options.content: To cover unexpected costs that arise during the project
options.rationale: Correct: a contingency is a reserve for the unexpected.

options.content: To make the project finish earlier than planned
options.rationale: A contingency does not shorten the project.

options.content: To show the bank that no risk exists at all
options.rationale: A contingency recognises that risk exists.

explanation: A contingency allows for unexpected costs without stopping the project.
hints: Think about what happens if prices rise or deliveries are late.

stem: Which question belongs to the **evaluation** stage of a project?

options.content: Which project ideas should be listed at the very beginning?
options.rationale: That belongs to identification.

options.content: How much material should be bought for the next week?
options.rationale: That is part of implementation.

options.content: Did the project meet its objective on time and budget?
options.rationale: Correct: evaluation compares results with the objective, time and budget.

options.content: Who will be invited to approve the written proposal?
options.rationale: That belongs to formulation.

explanation: Evaluation looks back at results, time and cost.
hints: Evaluation looks back at what has been done.

stem: Which is the **best-supported** judgement on whether a group should choose the project with the highest weighted score?

options.content: Yes, because a scoring matrix is always completely accurate in use
options.rationale: A matrix depends on judgements, which may be wrong.

options.content: No, because a project should be chosen without any comparison at all
options.rationale: A comparison improves the decision.

options.content: Yes, if the scores and weights are realistic and have been checked
options.rationale: Correct: the matrix helps, but its inputs are judgements.

options.content: No, because the weights in a scoring matrix have no value at all
options.rationale: Weights show what matters most and are useful if sensible.

explanation: A matrix supports a decision, but the result depends on the quality of the scores and weights.
hints: Choose the answer that is conditional on the quality of the scores.

stem: Evaluation is the last stage of the project cycle.
explanation: True. After implementation the team compares results with the objective, time and budget and records lessons.

stem: A project plan is written after the project has been completed.
explanation: False. The plan is written before implementation to set out activities, timetable and budget; the evaluation report is written after the project ends.
hints: Think about when the group needs to know what to do and when.

stem: Match each stage of the project cycle to its main activity.

right.content: Obtaining resources and carrying out the activities
Comparing results with the objective and recording lessons
Spotting a need and listing project ideas
Choosing an idea and writing the proposal, plan and budget

explanation: Each stage has a different purpose.

stem: Choose the correct word for each gap.

payload.template: A project {{blank:a}} sets out the activities, timetable and budget, while a {{blank:b}} is a reserve for unexpected costs.

explanation: The plan sets out how the project will be carried out; a contingency covers unexpected cost.

stem: State **one** criterion that a group could use to choose between project ideas.
explanation: Demand, cost, skills, resources, timing and risk are the usual criteria.

stem: A group scores a fictional poultry project 4 for demand (weight 50%), 3 for cost (weight 30%) and 5 for skills (weight 20%). What is its weighted score out of 5? Give your answer to one decimal place.
explanation: (4 × 50 + 3 × 30 + 5 × 20) ÷ 100 = (200 + 90 + 100) ÷ 100 = 3.9. Adding the scores and dividing by 3 ignores the weights and gives 4.0.
workedSolution: 1. (4 × 50 + 3 × 30 + 5 × 20) ÷ 100 = (200 + 90 + 100) ÷ 100 = 3.9. Adding the scores and dividing by 3 ignores the weights and gives 4.0.
hints: Multiply each score by its weight, add them, then divide by 100.

stem: The budget of a fictional mushroom project is US\$420 for materials, US\$180 for equipment, US\$90 for transport and US\$60 for advertising. The group adds a contingency of 10% of these costs. What is the total project budget?
explanation: Subtotal = 420 + 180 + 90 + 60 = 750. Contingency = 10% of 750 = 75. Total = 750 + 75 = US\$825. Leaving out the contingency gives US\$750.
workedSolution: 1. Subtotal = 420 + 180 + 90 + 60 = 750. Contingency = 10% of 750 = 75. Total = 750 + 75 = US\$825. Leaving out the contingency gives US\$750.
hints: Add the items, then find 10% of the subtotal.

stem: A fictional school project earned US\$1,560 in sales and cost US\$1,200 to run. Calculate the profit as a percentage of the amount spent. Give your answer to one decimal place.
explanation: Profit = 1,560 − 1,200 = US\$360. Profit as a percentage of cost = 360 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = 30.0%. Dividing by sales gives 23.1%.
workedSolution: 1. Profit = 1,560 − 1,200 = US\$360. Profit as a percentage of cost = 360 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = 30.0%. Dividing by sales gives 23.1%.
hints: Profit is income minus the amount spent.

stem: Explain why a group should evaluate its project when it has finished.

points.description: To find out whether the objective, time and budget were met
To record lessons that will improve future projects

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The group needs to find out whether the project met its objective, time and budget. It also records lessons so that future projects are better planned.

explanation: Two purposes of evaluation.

stem: A group of Form 5 students in Gweru is choosing between a vegetable garden and a car-wash project. Explain **two** factors they should consider before choosing.

points.description: Demand: how many customers will buy vegetables or car washes
Application: they could survey neighbours or passing cars
Resources and skills: water, land, tools and knowledge of gardening
Application: a garden needs water and several months to grow, while a car wash needs a supply of water and buckets

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: They should consider demand, perhaps by asking neighbours whether they would buy vegetables or use a car wash. They should also consider resources: a garden needs land, water and months to grow, while a car wash needs a water supply and buckets and can start earning at once.

explanation: Two factors, each applied to the two ideas.
hints: Think about customers, resources and time.

stem: Analyse why poor record keeping during a project makes evaluation difficult.

points.description: Without records the group cannot tell actual sales and costs
It cannot compare results with the budget
It cannot tell which activities caused delays or waste
So lessons for the future are unreliable

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Without records the group cannot tell what it really sold and spent, so it cannot compare results with the budget. It cannot find out which activities caused delay or waste, so the lessons for the next project are unreliable.

explanation: A chain from missing records to unreliable lessons.
hints: Think about what an evaluation compares.

stem: Evaluate whether a group should always choose the project with the highest expected profit.

points.description: Profit is a key reason for an enterprise project
Higher profit projects may need more money and skills
Higher profit may also carry more risk
The group may have other aims, such as learning or service
Judgement with a reason or condition

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Profit matters in an enterprise project, but a high-profit idea may need more money and skills than the group has and may carry more risk. The group may also value learning or service. It should choose the highest-profit project only if it can afford it, has the skills and can bear the risk; otherwise a safer project is better.

explanation: Both sides and a conditional judgement.
hints: Weigh profit against resources, risk and other aims.

stem: A fictional business: the Form 6 enterprise group at a school in Mutare plans a project to sell fruit juice at the school sports day. The budget is US\$300 for fruit and sugar, US\$150 for bottles, US\$60 for posters and US\$40 for transport. The group adds a contingency of 10% of the costs. It expects to sell 500 bottles at US\$1.50 each.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the total project budget including the contingency.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the expected profit if all 500 bottles are sold and the whole budget is spent.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain **one** risk to the project and how the group could reduce it.

points.description: Risk: bad weather or low attendance means fewer sales
Reduce by pre-selling to teachers or ordering fewer bottles first
Or keep some stock for later days to avoid waste

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Bad weather or low attendance would mean fewer sales. The group could pre-sell juice to teachers and order only part of the bottles at first, so that waste is limited.

parts.explanation: A risk and a way to reduce it.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State **two** questions the group should ask when evaluating the project.

points.description: Was the profit target met?
Was the project completed within the budget and on time?

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Was the profit target met, and was the project completed within the budget and on time?

explanation: The budget and the profit are calculated, a risk is explained and evaluation questions are given.
hints: The contingency is 10% of the subtotal.

stem: A fictional business: the Business Enterprise Skills class at a school in Chinhoyi has US\$800 to start a project. Three ideas are on the table: a school uniform repair service, a poultry project and a stationery shop. Demand is highest for stationery, but the shop needs US\$1,100 to start. The poultry project would need a hired shed and has taken three months to produce income in other classes. The uniform repair service needs only US\$250 and the class has three students with sewing skills, but the school is small and only about 150 pupils might use it.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain why the stationery shop is difficult for the class to start.

points.description: It needs US\$1,100 to start
The class has only US\$800
So it cannot afford it unless it finds extra funds

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The shop needs US\$1,100 to start, but the class has only US\$800, so it cannot afford it without extra funds.

parts.explanation: The cost compared with the funds.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Analyse **one** limitation of the poultry project for this class.

points.description: It takes three months to produce income
The class may not have enough time in the school year
It also needs a hired shed, adding cost

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The poultry project takes three months to produce income, so the class might not have enough time to earn and evaluate within the school year. It also needs a hired shed, which adds cost.

parts.explanation: Time and cost limit the poultry idea.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Evaluate which project the class should choose.

points.description: Uniform repair: low cost, has skills, but limited demand
Stationery: strong demand but cost exceeds funds
Poultry: slow and needs extra cost
Criteria: demand, cost, skills, time and risk
The class could start repairs and add stationery later from profit
A reasoned recommendation
A condition or time-frame

levels.descriptor: Describes the ideas with little comparison.
Compares the ideas using the case.
A justified recommendation with a condition.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The uniform repair service costs only US\$250 and uses skills the class already has, but demand is limited to about 150 pupils. The stationery shop has the strongest demand but costs more than the class can afford, and the poultry project is slow and needs a hired shed. The class should choose the uniform repair service because it fits their money and skills, and could add a small stationery stall from its profit later, provided that a survey confirms enough pupils will use the repair service.

parts.explanation: Ideas compared against the class's resources, with a conditional recommendation.
hints: Compare the ideas against demand, cost, skills and time, then recommend with a condition.

explanation: The constraints are explained and the choice of project is evaluated.
hints: Use the money, time and skills in the case.
